title: Gratitude and the Union of Practice and Knowledge
english: and they may not endure the insults. When I give great repentance concerning sins, then the thoughts, enlarging the struggles of the labors, diminish the sins, and often they cover them in secrecy, or even signify that these are permitted to remain, so that one might be discouraged by the labors, not calculating that the laments cried out because of the stings should be more numerous.

Chapter 14. But he who, cutting off the passions that fall upon him, commands more soldiers, will lead a campaign in the battle. Do not forget having stumbled, even if you repent, but have remembrance of your sin, the grief toward your humility, so that, having been humbled, you may by necessity cut off pride. If anyone having done impious things would wish to live excellently, let him stand in alternation of better things against the contrary of his deeds; for indeed he who opposes the contrary deed with the virtue of each, shoots the dragon with the quiver of virtues, and vanity is the sharpest weapon against the beast, piercing the labors, which he, having anticipated through the secret strategies of works, has approached all the bringing of the head of the devil. Seal your fragrances of the labors with silence, so that being released by the tongue, glory may steal them away; hide your tongue in the manner of the practical aspect of asceticism; for indeed, by silencing, your faithful companions witness the labors of your life. He who, not having anything from the present labors to be witnessed, let him never witness to himself by tongue; for some, having exhausted themselves through the labors of hardness of heart, compare their deeds as a cover for the laziness of past times, providing uncertain witnesses not present through manifest works. Just as you hide your sins from men, so hide the labors from them; for indeed the counter-art of the secrets of the heart, folding up the hidden things, and the refreshments, stand against them; but if we hide the faults with safety, and the pains against them we uncertainly reveal, we are performing the opposites in both. But be ashamed of the publication of shameful things, lest they make a reproach and render the things of your soul useless. Fear also the display of the labors, lest he bring the destruction of the soul as a man-pleasing accusation; but if you manifest the shameful things to God alone...
Regarding faults, do not display the struggles against them as if they were human victories, so that they might not be thought to be crowns.

Chapter 15. Those receiving the power of labors from grace should not think they have this as an inherent strength; for the word of the commandments is the cause of all good things to us, just as the one who casts away is the cause of all evil. Therefore, whatever good thing you accomplish, offer thanksgiving to the cause of the good; but whatever evil flows through you, cast it toward the leader of these. To the end of every undertaking, we bring thanksgiving to the better, so that your offering, being legally presented, the evil might be put to shame. For he who has joined thanksgiving to his practice will have an unshakeable treasure of the heart, having doubled the wall against evil. This man is praiseworthy, who has joined the contemplative to the practical, so that the space of the soul might water itself toward virtue from both sources; for the contemplative gives wings to the spiritual essence through the contemplation of the superior ones, but the practical kills the members upon the earth: fornication, the passion of uncleanness, evil, and bad desire. Therefore, those being surrounded by the armor of both these things will easily overcome the remaining wickedness of the demons. The demons fight the soul through thoughts, but those fight back more fiercely through endurance, and, being cowardly, they approach the rest of the battle wearing the strong general of the struggle. If you wish to command against the phalanx of the demons, shut the gates of your soul with stillness, and touch also your ear with the words of the fatherhood, so that then, having learned the thorns of thoughts, you might strike them, upon hearing paternal instruction. Do not be a judge of works, but an examiner of words.

Chapter 16. For it is the habit of such thoughts to lead you toward the practical aspect of the one instructing you, so that, having made you a terrible critic of this, they might turn you away from beneficial instruction. Do not contradict the one instructing, even if you are a contemplative; for if the practical of the contemplative is severed, the need of the one joining the harmony of either of the virtues will be judged by a terrible judgment. He who spreads the paternal commandment from the ear, and will be obedient to the legal commandment, shall not only speak being delighted by the achievements of the Fathers, but also himself being a worker of these.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Envy and the Deception of Satan
english: Demand the most wicked thing. He who seeks the more wicked thing is able to see what sort of thought opposes him with what sort of labor; he is found a craftsman in wrestling against error, but in all your noetic labors, if he should fail in any, the one who has seized this enters in its place. Remember to preserve the heart by the mindfulness of labors, lest the forgetfulness of the superior care, having seized it, deliver it to the captivity of the thoughts; for the forgetfulness of captivity leaps upon evil, so that, once the mind is stolen by it, this evil may readily enter in, the mind being stolen from God and distanced from memory, and sinning indifferently through the external senses; for such a one is unable to discipline hearing and tongue, because he has released the love-charm of labors from the outward senses. He who loves to listen to the one who blames so-and-so — the two work together with two complicit spirits; for evil-hearing becomes a partner of accusation, and they love one another unto the ruin of the heart.

Chapter 17. Bar your ears from slanders, so that you may not sin doubly with them, accustoming yourself to a terrible passion, and not restraining them from tongue-pain. The lover of mockery plunders the soul of the superior ones, digging through a rotten hearing with slanders; but he who flees the neighbor’s insulting tongue also puts his own insult to flight; he who provides pleasant ears to the mocker milks the venom of the beast into his ears. Let your ear not taste this bitter antidote, lest perhaps you also mix such a thing for another; do not bewitch your ear with slanders, so that, having been sold to passion, you may not serve through many sufferings; for one passion of the many, finding a place in you, brings in other things also to the same fold; then the ruler is enslaved by a multitude of evils, when, yoked to passion, he unyokes the labors. He who tries to search out the thoughts of others does not search out his own actions in deed; do not mock the one who has died as if he lived carelessly, so that you may not become a bitter judge of the dead from habit of the living. Do not let those who stumble exalt you with a vainglorious thought as a judge, but attend to yourself with a sober thought, and be a tester of your own actions. Groan as one stumbling, and do not puff up as one standing upright; be unobserved and do not boast, so that you may not clothe yourself in evil as an ornament. For some, unable to be known out of reverence, hastened, even if...

So that evil may be known in this way: others, having increased in envy, use accusations as grazing animals, and they belittle those standing firm in virtues. Some, gossiping about trivialities around you, shroud a noble life, not so that they might mourn trivial faults with toil, but so that they might shadow the reputations of the vainglorious.

But do not be beautified by the one deceiving you, nor be delighted by being deceived; for if he touches upon the serious merely for a name, he works not for God, but for men. Do not speak with boldness to the one living only for appearance, even if he sends a great name for this. He is a friend for the sake of a face, and time becomes his accuser.

Chapter 18. Beware of acquiring a friend to spy, so that you may find a cover for your own faults, and hide the envy existing in you rather than the envier. When your own friend, being diminished by your praises regarding your labors, turns toward envy, as if to hurl words of vainglory against your labors to those around you, so that he might shadow the glory running about you with his own limbs, then do not be moved by his malice, so that you may not siphon a bitter venom into your soul. For this is the work of Satan, to set him on fire with envy and to consume you with bitterness.

Rather let us humble ourselves, and let us lead such people in honor by enduring them, and by the table the thought made savage by zeal. Do not reproach the friend with zeal as if from another person, so that, by reproaching him as if from a different mouth, you might make yourself appear innocent and exalt yourself as blameless. For this is a transformation of Satan, of one seemingly reproaching the Most High from a face, so that, by reproaching his own envy toward God as if from another mouth, he himself is considered faultless.

Do not desire to have the brother as a slave, seeking to catch the fault of this one, so that you may not be found a fellow-worker with Satan. He who has faulted, and says others are faulting, or says ‘let him not fault if he is faulting,’ does so so that he may not be the only one fallen into evil, which is, first of all, from the fall of the devil, this also a work. But let him be one repenting of the strange works he has done; recognizing the lamentation of sorrow over them, he shall also embrace the primary stillness of labors, which appears to him as the manifold contemplation of virtues. Let him who is still in tongue be manly according to the thoughts; for the courage of the soul is not...

title: On Avoiding Human Praise and Cultivating Scripture
english: to suffer with, and to suffer in soul.

Chapter 19. Let not mouth alone, but also heart be guarded, for at times the eye of the soul is dimmed by the eye of people-pleasing, when the mind rests. Let your mind be blind toward the most shameful things, for the Lord makes such blind ones wise, but keen-sighted toward the most beautiful things, so that it may be blind toward the worst things. Consider for me that there are two fornications yoked in distinction, that of the body and that of the spirit; when a thought of fornication mingles with your spirit, then your soul consorts with an imprint of error. A demon is formed with a woman’s face, to drug the soul into mingling with it; a bodiless demon wears a carved form, to prostitute the soul with an undisciplined thought. Do not, then, veil yourself with a non-existent idol, lest you do the like also in the flesh — such as these were led astray by a spirit of fornication, who do not scare away the inner adulteries of the spirits with the cross. Torment the thoughts with abstinence from foods, so that they speak not of fornication but of hunger; establish tears by wakefulness in prayer, so that you may receive help for the present war. In the time of the war of fornication, decline the invitations of hosts, and you will give rest to the stranger who stands by, serving him, but yourself, in a veiled manner, you will fence about with abstinence. Let your reward for both works be double, apportioning to each one the practical through virtue; do not eat with the brother for the sake of the belly, but for Christ’s sake lodge together with love. Satiety of foods feeds thoughts, and drunkenness gives drink of sleep to phantasy. Pleasure has died after the gorge of luxury, and in the tomb breathe the lewdnesses of the belly. The labors of the allotment end in rest, but the ways of luxury end in burning. He who withers the flower of the flesh by asceticism meditates daily in the flesh upon his own end. Let the reckoning of the heart measure the body, so that, if it is struck, it may not also grow weary; let the flesh be content to cut off natural things; let your bodily exercise be managed among the habits, so that you may learn to toil with the heart and to suffer with the soul.

Chapter 20. Let those who make the appearance of virtue shine in their training cast away this thought, to come to the praise of men, and let them cast it inward before the encounter. When you abstain from wine, and oil, and superfluous things for a period of time, then the thoughts calculate the times for you with praises, suggesting that you are enduring pains for the sake of those training the body. It is fitting, then, that you should answer back to the ill-disposed ones who have calculated [your merits], with whatever stands against the reversal of their foolishness. Which of the brothers, being praised inwardly for his pains against demons, sang: ‘Let them turn away immediately, being ashamed, those saying to me: Well done! Well done!’ (Matt 25:21). Let not the thought bring a many-year cycle upon you in your life of solitude, so that they might not hang your pains upon the years, nor might you be depicted as boasting in the endurance of the desert; but let it be remembered in the endurance of the worthlessness of a slave to be useless.

Because of old age, someone was forcing a certain venerable desert-dweller, a long-enduring one, to take him. And he to him said: ‘Stop, he says, the violence, for the evildoer has not been called to exile yet.’ And while this man was seeking from me the word of instruction, he said: ‘Seek, first, the innate fear through experience, and then you will find within the experienced word, the man teaching knowledge.’ And the same, being questioned also about fear, answered thus: ‘He having the care of the memory of death, is led also into the fear of judgment.’ Become a companion to the fear of the Divine Scriptures at every moment; for by the company of these [Scriptures], you will lead out the conversation of thoughts. The one treasuring the Divine Scriptures by meditation in the heart, easily casts out the thoughts from this. While listening to the Divine [Scriptures] in nocturnal readings during vigils, let us not kill the ears with sleep, nor betray the soul to the captivity of thoughts, but let us moisten the heart with the center of the Scriptures, so that by the moistening of care we may divide the opposite neglect.

Chapter 21. Some, I say, through reputation, and not through care of the soul, are loved by the pious, so that they may acquire for themselves a world only; but he who is burning through love by the memory of heavenly things, [casts out] the approval of earthly things from the intention...
